questions.q: What does the Azure SQL firewall check, and when does that check happen relative to login?
options: It checks the source IP address of the connection attempt, and rejects it before authentication is even attempted if the IP isn't allow-listed
It checks the user's password strength after login succeeds
It checks the query text for SQL injection patterns after the connection is established
It only applies to database-level rules, never server-level rules
questions.explain: The firewall is a layer before login — a rejected IP never gets far enough to attempt a password.

questions.q: What is the real difference between a server-level and a database-level firewall rule?
options: A server-level rule applies to every database on the logical server; a database-level rule is scoped to just one database and is managed from inside that database
They are identical in scope — the names are interchangeable
A database-level rule applies to every server in the subscription
Server-level rules only work with Entra ID authentication
questions.explain: Database-level rules are useful when different databases on the same server need different allowed IP ranges, like a vendor's reporting-only access.

questions.q: What actually happens when you turn on "Allow Azure services and resources to access this server"?
options: It opens the firewall to any Azure resource in any Azure subscription — not just your own — relying entirely on login/auth to do the real access control from there
It allows only the Azure resources inside your own subscription to connect
It has no security effect at all and is purely cosmetic
It automatically restricts access to a specific virtual network
questions.explain: Azure doesn't verify the connecting resource is yours — it's a convenience switch, not a trusted-resource switch.

questions.q: Where can you view a server's configured server-level firewall rules with T-SQL?
options: SELECT * FROM sys.firewall_rules;
SELECT * FROM sys.database_permissions;
SELECT * FROM sys.server_principals;
EXEC sp_helpuser;
questions.explain: sys.firewall_rules lives in master and lists every server-level rule configured on that logical server.

questions.q: Why does getting the firewall configuration wrong undermine everything configured in Chapter 4 (logins, roles, GRANT/DENY)?
options: Because the firewall runs before login — a rejected connection never reaches the point where any login or permission rule could even be evaluated
It doesn't undermine anything; firewall rules and permissions are fully independent and both always get evaluated
Because GRANT and DENY only take effect after the firewall is disabled
Because firewall rules override GRANT permissions even for allowed IPs
questions.explain: The firewall is the earliest, coarsest gate — get it wrong and correctly-scoped permissions downstream never even get a chance to apply.
